correctness.rationale: For every odd \(b\ge3\), the low \(2b+1\) multiples \(L_j=1+j(b-1)\) have digit sum either \(1\) or \(b\). CRT chooses \(P\) such that \(P\) and \(Q=P-(b-1)\) have no prime factors at most \(U=1+2b(b-1)\), compatibly with \(P\equiv1\pmod b\) and \(P\equiv-1\pmod{b-1}\). With \(K=P-b\), \(a=(P+b)/(b-1)\), and \(R=K-a\ge0\), the separated one-digit sum \(C\) has digit sum \(K\) and residue \(2P\pmod{PQ}\). Multiplicative-order shifts \(N=C b^m+1\) yield digit sums \(P\) or \(Q\), and the corresponding residues reduce to \(L_j\) or \(L_j+2(b-1)\), both at most \(U\), forcing all gcds to be one. Unlimited choices of \(m\) yield distinct starts. Full-integer checks at bases \(3,5\) and modular checks at ten bases succeeded; finite experiments are not treated as an infinite proof.

originality.rationale: The motivating full arXiv text proves the exact \(2b+1\) maximum for even bases and the corresponding lower bound for odd prime bases, but not odd composite bases. Its arbitrary-length result varies the difference, whereas the present result fixes it to \(b-1\); its prime-obstruction bound is inapplicable to this step. No published-finding corpus record or targeted literature result supplying the composite case was identified; unindexed coverage and the journal full text remain stated risks.

value.rationale: The fixed difference \(b-1\) and length \(2b+1\) are exactly the published benchmark: even \(b\) has an exact maximum, and odd prime \(b\) has the corresponding lower bound. Extension to every odd composite base fills a natural parameter gap which the former prime-only argument could not cover. The new construction proves infinitude through a two-level digital profile and CRT avoidance of all small prime factors, rather than merely listing examples. The odd-base maximum remains undetermined.
